title: What is Java?
content: Java was created by James Gosling at Sun Microsystems in 1995. Today it powers Android apps, banking systems, Netflix, Amazon, and Spring Boot backends.
The three essential components: JDK (Java Development Kit), JRE (Java Runtime Environment), and JVM (Java Virtual Machine).

title: Hello, World!
tagline: Your very first Java program — dissected
content: In Java, every piece of code must live inside a class. The class name must match the filename.
Breaking down public static void main(String[] args) — the JVM entry point.

title: Variables & Data Types
tagline: Java's typed boxes for storing data
content: Java has 8 primitive types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean.
Reference types live on the heap: String, arrays, and objects you create.

title: Operators
content: Java supports arithmetic (+ - * / %), comparison (== != > < >= <=), and logical (&& || !) operators.
Be careful with integer division: 7 / 2 == 3 in Java; use 7.0 / 2 for decimal division.

title: Strings
content: Strings in Java are immutable — methods like toUpperCase() return a new String.
Use StringBuilder for efficient concatenation in loops.

title: If/Else & Switch
content: if/else chains and switch statements control program flow.
Use modern switch expressions (Java 14+) to avoid fall-through bugs.

title: Loops
content: Loops let you repeat actions. for-each is best when you don't need the index.
Watch for infinite loops if the exit condition never becomes false.

title: Arrays & Methods
content: Arrays are fixed-size sequences. Use methods to structure behavior and visualize the call stack.
Pass-by-value for primitives, object references are passed by value of the reference.

title: Classes & Objects
content: A class defines fields and methods; objects are instances. Use private fields and public getters/setters to encapsulate.
Constructors initialize new objects and this refers to the instance.

title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
content: Inheritance allows a subclass to extend a superclass. Polymorphism lets you treat subclasses as their parent type.
Prefer composition over inheritance for flexible designs.

title: Collections Intro
content: Learn ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap, HashSet and when to use each.
Collections framework provides common interfaces and implementations for working with groups of objects.
code:
import java.util.*;
public class CollectionsIntro{ public static void main(String[] args){ List<String> l = new ArrayList<>(); l.add("a"); System.out.println(l.get(0)); } }

title: Exceptions
content: Use try/catch/finally to handle exceptions. Throw custom exceptions for domain errors.
Understand checked vs unchecked exceptions.
code: public class ExceptionsDemo{ public static void main(String[] args){ try{ int x = 1/0; } catch(Exception e){ System.out.println("Error: "+e.getMessage()); } } }

title: File I/O
content: Use Files, BufferedReader, BufferedWriter, and try-with-resources to manage resources.
Prefer NIO (Files and Path) for modern file operations.
code:
import java.nio.file.*;
public class FileIO{ public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception{ Files.writeString(Path.of("note.txt"), "hello"); System.out.println(Files.readString(Path.of("note.txt"))); } }
